claim: Transdiagnostic compulsivity (CIT) is associated with impaired metacognition.
source: CIT is associated with impaired metacognition, which in turn has been associated with cognitive offloading behaviours such as external reminder setting that play a key role in fulfilling cognitive goals.
evidence: The abstract states this relationship directly, and it is supported by citations to previous research throughout the manuscript.

claim: Impaired metacognition has been associated with cognitive offloading behaviours such as external reminder setting.
source: CIT is associated with impaired metacognition, which in turn has been associated with cognitive offloading behaviours such as external reminder setting that play a key role in fulfilling cognitive goals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Compulsive individuals had reduced preference for external reminders.
source: Compulsive individuals had reduced preference for external reminders.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analyses presented in the results section.

claim: The reduced preference for external reminders in compulsive individuals was partially, but not fully, attributable to their relative overconfidence.
source: This was partially, but not fully, attributable to their relative overconfidence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through mediation analysis in the results.

claim: There was no evidence for an impaired confidence-action link in compulsive individuals.
source: In contrast to previous studies, we found no evidence for an impaired confidence-action link: compulsive individuals used their metacognition to guide offloading just as much as their non-compulsive counterparts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analyses showing no significant interaction effect in the results section.

claim: Compulsive individuals are at increased risk of inadequate external memory support.
source: Given the compensatory nature of cognitive offloading, our findings imply that compulsive individuals are at increased risk of inadequate external memory support.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that compulsive individuals use fewer reminders despite the compensatory benefits of cognitive offloading.

claim: Transdiagnostic phenotypes can be extracted from extensive symptom datasets using factor analysis.
source: Using factor analysis, temporally stable (see Fox et al., 2023; Sookud et al., 2024), transdiagnostic phenotypes can be extracted from extensive symptom datasets (Wise et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Transdiagnostic phenotypes are temporally stable.
source: Using factor analysis, temporally stable (see Fox et al., 2023; Sookud et al., 2024), transdiagnostic phenotypes can be extracted from extensive symptom datasets (Wise et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to Fox et al., 2023 and Sookud et al., 2024.

claim: Transdiagnostic traits are not confined to a single clinical diagnosis but can span a range of conditions.
source: These traits are not confined to a single clinical diagnosis but instead can span a range of conditions, at the same time addressing the diagnostic heterogeneity within conditions, such as obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD; e.g. Gillan et al., 2016; Wise and Dolan, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Transdiagnostic compulsivity is linked to impairments in metacognition.
source: Previous research links transdiagnostic compulsivity to impairments in metacognition, defined as thinking about one's own thoughts, encompassing a broad spectrum of self-reflective signals, such as feelings of confidence (e.g. Rouault et al., 2018; Seow and Gillan, 2020; Benwell et al., 2022; Fox et al., 2023; Fox et al., 2024; Hoven et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Metacognitive signals such as feelings of confidence guide cognitive offloading strategies like setting external reminders.
source: Other studies have shown that metacognitive signals such as feelings of confidence guide cognitive offloading strategies like setting external reminders as memory aids (e.g. Gilbert, 2015; Boldt and Gilbert, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cognitive offloading plays an integral role in daily lives and is a key contributor to effectiveness as cognitive agents.
source: This matters because cognitive offloading plays an integral role in our daily lives and is a key contributor to our effectiveness as cognitive agents (Gilbert et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: By offloading memory demands, individuals increase the likelihood of successfully completing tasks.
source: By offloading memory demands this way, we not only increase the likelihood of successfully completing tasks (Boldt and Gilbert, 2019), but we may also free up cognitive resources for other activities (Dupont et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Offloading memory demands may free up cognitive resources for other activities.
source: By offloading memory demands this way, we not only increase the likelihood of successfully completing tasks (Boldt and Gilbert, 2019), but we may also free up cognitive resources for other activities (Dupont et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: People tend to set more reminders when they feel less confident.
source: People tend to set more reminders when they feel less confident.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The link between confidence and offloading holds even after taking into account actual memory ability.
source: In other words, people tend to set reminders when they think that they will forget, and this effect holds even after taking into account actual memory ability (e.g. Boldt and Gilbert, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The link between confidence and offloading is observed both for situational fluctuations in confidence due to varying task difficulties (state variable) and for a general predisposition towards over- or underconfidence (trait variable).
source: The link between confidence and offloading is observed both for situational fluctuations in confidence due to varying task difficulties (state variable; Boldt and Gilbert, 2022) and for a general predisposition towards over- or underconfidence (trait variable; Boldt and Gilbert, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Individuals characterised by transdiagnostic compulsivity have been consistently found to exhibit overconfidence.
source: More specifically, individuals characterised by transdiagnostic compulsivity have been consistently found to exhibit overconfidence (Rouault et al., 2018; Seow and Gillan, 2020; Benwell et al., 2022; Fox et al., 2023; Fox et al., 2024; Hoven et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Underconfidence is more common in patients with OCD than overconfidence.
source: However, while transdiagnostic compulsivity is liked to overconfidence, the opposite pattern of underconfidence is more common in patients with OCD, a compulsive disorder (as reviewed in Hoven et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Metacognitive impairments in transdiagnostic compulsivity and OCD may originate from different mechanisms.
source: Recent research suggests that metacognitive impairments in transdiagnostic compulsivity and OCD may originate from different mechanisms (Hoven et al., 2023b; Hoven et al., 2023c), advising caution against broad generalisations between these groups.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The composite measure of transdiagnostic compulsivity includes questionnaire items linked not only with OCD but also other clinical conditions such as eating disorders.
source: It should also be noted that the composite measure of transdiagnostic compulsivity includes questionnaire items linked not only with OCD but also other clinical conditions such as eating disorders (Tasca et al., 2011; Gillan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Individuals high in transdiagnostic compulsivity and those with a diagnosis of OCD show similar impairments in metacognitive control, characterised by a disrupted connection between confidence and future actions.
source: Despite opposite trends in metacognitive monitoring performance (under- versus overconfidence), individuals high in transdiagnostic compulsivity and those with a diagnosis of OCD show similar impairments in metacognitive control, characterised by a disrupted connection between confidence and future actions (Seow and Gillan, 2020; Vaghi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Metacognitive impairments are central to explanations of compulsive behaviours, notably in OCD patients.
source: Metacognitive impairments are also central to explanations of compulsive behaviours, notably in OCD patients.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In OCD patients, compulsivity can manifest in the form of checking behaviours.
source: In such patients, compulsivity can manifest in the form of checking behaviours, e.g., checking that doors are locked or that appliances are switched off (Den Ouden et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Checking behaviours are present in other compulsive disorders such as 'body checking' in eating disorders.
source: Whilst checking behaviours are also present in other compulsive disorders (e.g. 'body checking' in eating disorders; Mountford et al., 2006), in OCD, these checks are often repetitive and ritualised and are typically associated with obsessive thoughts.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In OCD, checking behaviours are often repetitive and ritualised and are typically associated with obsessive thoughts.
source: Whilst checking behaviours are also present in other compulsive disorders (e.g. 'body checking' in eating disorders; Mountford et al., 2006), in OCD, these checks are often repetitive and ritualised and are typically associated with obsessive thoughts.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about OCD.

claim: OCD patients commonly report that checking compulsions have the aim of reducing anxiety generally, preventing a feared consequence from taking place, or that they are performed automatically and without thinking.
source: However, the exact function that checking compulsions serve is unclear; patients commonly report that they have the aim of reducing anxiety generally, preventing a feared consequence from taking place or that they are performed automatically and without thinking (Starcevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Some research argues that OCD patients' checking arises from low memory confidence despite intact memory.
source: Some research argues that OCD patients' checking arises from low memory confidence despite intact memory (Tolin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: A reminder can serve as a future checkpoint that allows us to revisit a task at an appropriate time to complete it.
source: In other words, a reminder can serve as a future checkpoint that allows us to revisit a task at an appropriate time to complete it, perhaps by setting an alarm on our phone, jotting down a note, or strategically placing a related object somewhere visible.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents a conceptual understanding of reminder function.

claim: More compulsive individuals tend to have impaired metacognitive control, meaning they use metacognitive signals to a lesser extent to guide future behaviour.
source: First is the Metacognitive Control Mechanism: Previous research has found that more compulsive individuals tend to have impaired metacognitive control (Seow and Gillan, 2020), meaning they use metacognitive signals to a lesser extent to guide future behaviour.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Similar deficits in metacognitive control have been observed in case-control studies comparing OCD patients with healthy controls examining how confidence and action are correlated.
source: Compulsivity is a hallmark symptom of OCD, and similar deficits in metacognitive control have been observed in a case-control studies comparing OCD patients with healthy controls examining how confidence and action are correlated (Vaghi et al., 2017; though see also Hoven et al., 2023b; Marzuki et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Prior evidence exists for overconfidence in compulsivity.
source: Prior evidence exists for overconfidence in compulsivity (Rouault et al., 2018; Seow and Gillan, 2020; Benwell et al., 2022; Fox et al., 2023; Fox et al., 2024; Hoven et al., 2023a), which would therefore result in fewer reminders.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Anxious-depression (AD) individuals typically display relative underconfidence.
source: Whereas compulsivity has been linked to increased confidence, AD individuals typically display relative underconfidence (Rouault et al., 2018; Seow and Gillan, 2020; Benwell et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: 600 participants drawn from the general population completed several individual differences questionnaires.
source: In the present preregistered study, we asked 600 participants drawn from the general population to complete several individual differences questionnaires.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and describes the study design.

claim: Questionnaire responses were weighted to produce both a 'CIT' factor and an 'AD' factor.
source: These responses were then weighted to produce both a 'CIT' factor and an 'AD' factor (Gillan et al., 2016; Wise and Dolan, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations describing the methodology.

claim: Participants performed a highly demanding, short-term memory task.
source: Participants performed a highly demanding, short-term memory task.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and describes the experimental task.

claim: On some trials, participants relied on internal memory alone, which typically resulted in poor accuracy.
source: On some trials, they relied on internal memory alone (which typically resulted in poor accuracy); on other trials, they could set external reminders (which dramatically improved accuracy).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and describes task performance.

claim: On some trials, participants could set external reminders, which dramatically improved accuracy.
source: On some trials, they relied on internal memory alone (which typically resulted in poor accuracy); on other trials, they could set external reminders (which dramatically improved accuracy).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and describes task performance.

claim: Correct responses always earned 10 points if participants used internal memory, but a lower number of points between 2 and 9 if they used external reminders.
source: Correct responses always earned 10 points if participants used internal memory, but a lower number of points between 2 and 9 if they used external reminders.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and describes the task design.

claim: Confidence varied positively with the CIT factor.
source: Previewing our results, in line with previous evidence, we found that confidence varied positively with the CIT factor and negatively with the AD factor.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a preview of results and is supported by statistical analyses in the results section.

claim: Confidence varied negatively with the AD factor.
source: Previewing our results, in line with previous evidence, we found that confidence varied positively with the CIT factor and negatively with the AD factor.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a preview of results and is supported by statistical analyses in the results section.

claim: More compulsive individuals offloaded less rather than more.
source: However, contrary to our initial expectations, more compulsive individuals offloaded less rather than more, and there was no evidence for disruption in the link between metacognition and offloading.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a preview of results and is supported by statistical analyses in the results section.

claim: There was no evidence for disruption in the link between metacognition and offloading in compulsive individuals.
source: However, contrary to our initial expectations, more compulsive individuals offloaded less rather than more, and there was no evidence for disruption in the link between metacognition and offloading.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a preview of results and is supported by statistical analyses in the results section.

claim: A significant proportion of the reduced reminder setting in compulsive individuals could be attributed to overconfidence.
source: Instead, we discovered an incomplete mediation effect: while a significant proportion of the reduced reminder setting could be attributed to overconfidence, not all the variance was accounted for by this variable.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a preview of results and is supported by mediation analysis in the results section.

claim: Not all the variance in reduced reminder setting was accounted for by overconfidence.
source: Instead, we discovered an incomplete mediation effect: while a significant proportion of the reduced reminder setting could be attributed to overconfidence, not all the variance was accounted for by this variable.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a preview of results and is supported by mediation analysis in the results section.

claim: Even after controlling for overconfidence, compulsivity still predicted reduced reminder setting.
source: Even after controlling for it, compulsivity still predicted reduced reminder setting.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a preview of results and is supported by statistical analyses in the results section.

claim: 69 out of a total of 669 participants were excluded based on six preregistered criteria.
source: We excluded 69 out of a total of 669 participants based on our six preregistered criteria described in the Materials and methods section, leaving us with a final sample of 600 participants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and describes the data exclusion process.

claim: The final sample consisted of 600 participants.
source: We excluded 69 out of a total of 669 participants based on our six preregistered criteria described in the Materials and methods section, leaving us with a final sample of 600 participants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: 375 participants identified as male, 218 as female and 7 as other.
source: Three hundred and seventy-five participants identified as male, 218 as female and 7 as other.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and describes the sample demographics.

claim: Participants were on average 32.9 years of age (min = 18; max = 76).
source: Participants were on average 32.9 years of age (min = 18; max = 76).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and describes the sample demographics.

claim: Included participants had higher average performance when reminders were used (96.1%) compared to when people had to do the task unaided (59.2%).
source: Figure 1 shows the included (black) and excluded (red) data, with higher average performance for included participants when reminders were used (96.1%) compared to when people had to do the task unaided (59.2%).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The reminder bias and metacognitive bias are negatively correlated (r=–0.2, p<0.001).
source: There was indeed a significant negative correlation, r=–0.2, p<0.001 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The reminder bias was significantly greater than zero (m=0.52, t(599) = 5.1, p<0.001, d=0.21).
source: In other words, we expected the reminder bias to be greater than zero, which was indeed the case, m=0.52, t(599) = 5.1, p<0.001, d=0.21.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: Participants showed an average, negative metacognitive bias (m=–3.64, t(599) = –3.1, p=0.001, d=–0.13).
source: Our data supported this hypothesis, m=–3.64, t(599) = –3.1, p=0.001, d=–0.13.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: The OIP and AIP were positively correlated (r=0.36, p<0.001).
source: Indeed, the OIP and AIP were positively correlated, suggesting participants who benefited most from reminders were more likely to use them, r=0.36, p<0.001.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: Participants who benefited most from reminders were more likely to use them.
source: Indeed, the OIP and AIP were positively correlated, suggesting participants who benefited most from reminders were more likely to use them, r=0.36, p<0.001.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference from the positive correlation between OIP and AIP.

claim: The metacognitive bias correlated negatively with AD (β=–0.23, SE = 0.05, t=–4.99, p<0.001).
source: We found support for both hypotheses, both for AD, β=–0.23, SE = 0.05, t=–4.99, p<0.001, and CIT, β=0.15, SE = 0.05, t=3.11, p=0.002, controlling for age, gender, and educational attainment (Figure 3; see also Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The metacognitive bias correlated positively with CIT (β=0.15, SE = 0.05, t=3.11, p=0.002).
source: We found support for both hypotheses, both for AD, β=–0.23, SE = 0.05, t=–4.99, p<0.001, and CIT, β=0.15, SE = 0.05, t=3.11, p=0.002, controlling for age, gender, and educational attainment (Figure 3; see also Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support and shown in Figure 3.

claim: More compulsive individuals tend to be overconfident.
source: Note that for CIT, this effect was positive, and more compulsive individuals tend to be overconfident.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an interpretation of the positive correlation between CIT and metacognitive bias.

claim: Raw confidence correlated negatively with AD (β=–0.29, SE = 0.04, t=–6.43, p<0.001).
source: Indeed, the same patterns were found for both AD, β=–0.29, SE = 0.04, t=–6.43, p<0.001, and CIT, β=0.12, SE = 0.05, t=2.76, p=0.006 (see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: Raw confidence correlated positively with CIT (β=0.12, SE = 0.05, t=2.76, p=0.006).
source: Indeed, the same patterns were found for both AD, β=–0.29, SE = 0.04, t=–6.43, p<0.001, and CIT, β=0.12, SE = 0.05, t=2.76, p=0.006 (see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: Including scores from the cognitive ability test as an additional covariate did not change the results for the relationship between AD and metacognitive bias (β=–0.20, SE = 0.05, t=–4.46, p<0.001).
source: Including scores from the cognitive ability test as an additional covariate (Hypotheses H8c and H6c, respectively) furthermore did not change the results, AD, β=–0.20, SE = 0.05, t=–4.46, p<0.001; CIT, β=0.12, SE = 0.05, t=2.57, p=0.011 (see Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: Including scores from the cognitive ability test as an additional covariate did not change the results for the relationship between CIT and metacognitive bias (β=0.12, SE = 0.05, t=2.57, p=0.011).
source: Including scores from the cognitive ability test as an additional covariate (Hypotheses H8c and H6c, respectively) furthermore did not change the results, AD, β=–0.20, SE = 0.05, t=–4.46, p<0.001; CIT, β=0.12, SE = 0.05, t=2.57, p=0.011 (see Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: Compulsivity was linked to a significantly reduced reminder bias (β=–0.14, SE = 0.05, t=–2.91, p=0.004).
source: However, our results showed the exact opposite effect with a significantly reduced reminder bias in compulsive individuals, β=–0.14, SE = 0.05, t=–2.91, p=0.004, controlling for age, gender, and educational attainment (Figure 4; see also Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The trend of reduced offloading in compulsive individuals persisted when predicting the absolute number of reminders chosen (β=–0.09, SE = 0.05, t=–1.94, p=0.053).
source: This trend persisted when, instead, we predicted the absolute number of reminders chosen by the participant (Hypothesis H5b), β=–0.09, SE = 0.05, t=–1.94, p=0.053 (see Appendix 1—table 5), as well as when predicting the AIP (Hypothesis H5c), β=0.10, SE = 0.05, t=2.25, p=0.025 (see Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: The trend of reduced offloading in compulsive individuals persisted when predicting the AIP (β=0.10, SE = 0.05, t=2.25, p=0.025).
source: This trend persisted when, instead, we predicted the absolute number of reminders chosen by the participant (Hypothesis H5b), β=–0.09, SE = 0.05, t=–1.94, p=0.053 (see Appendix 1—table 5), as well as when predicting the AIP (Hypothesis H5c), β=0.10, SE = 0.05, t=2.25, p=0.025 (see Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: Previous studies have found reduced working memory in OCD.
source: Previous studies have found reduced working memory in OCD (Harkin and Kessler, 2011), which could potentially lead to increased reminder use in compulsivity.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The reduced reminder bias in compulsive individuals persisted if d' from the 2-back task was included as an additional covariate (β=–0.12, SE = 0.05, t=–2.57, p=0.010).
source: However, the reduced reminder bias persisted if d' from the 2-back task was included as an additional covariate (Hypothesis H5d), β=–0.12, SE = 0.05, t=–2.57, p=0.010 (see Appendix 1—table 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: The reduced reminder bias in compulsive individuals persisted when scores from the cognitive ability test were included as an additional covariate (β=–0.14, SE = 0.05, t=–2.85, p=0.005).
source: Finally, we predicted that our results would persist independent of whether or not the scores from the cognitive ability test were included as an additional covariate (Hypothesis H5e), which was indeed the case, β=–0.14, SE = 0.05, t=–2.85, p=0.005 (see Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: AD was not significantly linked to any changes in reminder bias (β=0.07, SE = 0.05, t=1.46, p=0.15).
source: AD was not significantly linked to any changes in reminder bias, β=0.07, SE = 0.05, t=1.46, p=0.15 (see Appendix 1—table 4), absolute number of reminders, β=0.06, SE = 0.05, t=1.33, p=0.18 (see Appendix 1—table 5), or AIP, β=–0.08, SE = 0.05, t=–1.76, p=0.08, (see Appendix 1—table 6) controlling for age, gender, and educational attainment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: AD was not significantly linked to absolute number of reminders (β=0.06, SE = 0.05, t=1.33, p=0.18).
source: AD was not significantly linked to any changes in reminder bias, β=0.07, SE = 0.05, t=1.46, p=0.15 (see Appendix 1—table 4), absolute number of reminders, β=0.06, SE = 0.05, t=1.33, p=0.18 (see Appendix 1—table 5), or AIP, β=–0.08, SE = 0.05, t=–1.76, p=0.08, (see Appendix 1—table 6) controlling for age, gender, and educational attainment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: AD was not significantly linked to AIP (β=–0.08, SE = 0.05, t=–1.76, p=0.08).
source: AD was not significantly linked to any changes in reminder bias, β=0.07, SE = 0.05, t=1.46, p=0.15 (see Appendix 1—table 4), absolute number of reminders, β=0.06, SE = 0.05, t=1.33, p=0.18 (see Appendix 1—table 5), or AIP, β=–0.08, SE = 0.05, t=–1.76, p=0.08, (see Appendix 1—table 6) controlling for age, gender, and educational attainment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: The null effect of AD on reminder bias did not change when working memory was included as an additional covariate (β=0.06, SE = 0.05, t=1.23, p=0.22).
source: This null effect did not change when working memory, β=0.06, SE = 0.05, t=1.23, p=0.22 (see Appendix 1—table 7), or scores from the cognitive ability test were included as additional covariates, β=0.07, SE = 0.05, t=1.41, p=0.16 (see Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: The null effect of AD on reminder bias did not change when scores from the cognitive ability test were included as an additional covariate (β=0.07, SE = 0.05, t=1.41, p=0.16).
source: This null effect did not change when working memory, β=0.06, SE = 0.05, t=1.23, p=0.22 (see Appendix 1—table 7), or scores from the cognitive ability test were included as additional covariates, β=0.07, SE = 0.05, t=1.41, p=0.16 (see Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: The interaction between metacognitive bias and compulsivity in a model predicting the reminder bias was not significant (β=–0.01, SE = 0.04, t=–0.18, p=0.86).
source: However, the interaction between metacognitive bias and compulsivity in a model predicting the reminder bias was not significant, β=–0.01, SE = 0.04, t=–0.18, p=0.86, controlling for age, gender, and educational attainment (see Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: In the task, confidence and offloading were linked just as much in high compulsive individuals as in their low compulsive counterparts.
source: This means that in our task, confidence and offloading were linked just as much as in their low compulsive counterparts.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an interpretation of the non-significant interaction effect.

claim: The non-significant interaction between metacognitive bias and compulsivity remained the same even if working memory performance was included as an additional covariate (β=–0.01, SE = 0.04, t=–0.26, p=0.79).
source: These results remained the same even if working memory performance (d' from the 2-back task) was included as an additional covariate (Hypothesis H7b), β=–0.01, SE = 0.04, t=–0.26, p=0.79 (see Appendix 1—table 10), or if scores from the cognitive ability test were included as an additional covariate (Hypothesis H7c), β=–0.01, SE = 0.04, t=–0.18, p=0.86 (see Appendix 1—table 11).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: The non-significant interaction between metacognitive bias and compulsivity remained the same even if scores from the cognitive ability test were included as an additional covariate (β=–0.01, SE = 0.04, t=–0.18, p=0.86).
source: These results remained the same even if working memory performance (d' from the 2-back task) was included as an additional covariate (Hypothesis H7b), β=–0.01, SE = 0.04, t=–0.26, p=0.79 (see Appendix 1—table 10), or if scores from the cognitive ability test were included as an additional covariate (Hypothesis H7c), β=–0.01, SE = 0.04, t=–0.18, p=0.86 (see Appendix 1—table 11).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: Parts of the reduction of reminders in compulsive individuals could be traced back to overconfidence (β=–0.19, SE = 0.04, t=–4.66, p<0.001).
source: Contrary to our initial hypotheses, we found that increased CIT was associated with decreased rather than increased bias towards offloading. Seeing as CIT was also associated with increased confidence, and high confidence predicts low bias towards offloading, we tested whether the relationship between CIT and offloading was mediated via confidence: whilst parts of the reduction of reminders could be traced back to overconfidence, β=–0.19, SE = 0.04, t=–4.66, p<0.001, there was still a significant proportion of variance that was linked to compulsivity independently of this effect, β=–0.10, SE = 0.05, t=–2.14, p=0.032.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support from mediation analysis.

claim: There was still a significant proportion of variance in reduced reminder setting that was linked to compulsivity independently of overconfidence (β=–0.10, SE = 0.05, t=–2.14, p=0.032).
source: Contrary to our initial hypotheses, we found that increased CIT was associated with decreased rather than increased bias towards offloading. Seeing as CIT was also associated with increased confidence, and high confidence predicts low bias towards offloading, we tested whether the relationship between CIT and offloading was mediated via confidence: whilst parts of the reduction of reminders could be traced back to overconfidence, β=–0.19, SE = 0.04, t=–4.66, p<0.001, there was still a significant proportion of variance that was linked to compulsivity independently of this effect, β=–0.10, SE = 0.05, t=–2.14, p=0.032.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support from mediation analysis.

source: Equally, we have already reported the effect of CIT on the mediator (the metacognitive bias), β=0.15, SE = 0.05, t=3.11, p=0.002.

claim: The indirect influence of the CIT factor on reminder bias going through the metacognitive bias was calculated to be (0.15) * (–0.19)=–0.0285.

source: The bootstrapped unstandardised indirect effect (the average causal mediation effect) computed to be –0.0256, with the 95% confidence interval ranging from –0.05 to –0.01.

claim: The indirect effect of CIT on reminder bias through metacognitive bias was statistically significant at p=0.002.
source: This indicated that the effect was statistically significant at p=0.002.

claim: There was no evidence for a moderation effect of AD (an interaction between AD scores and metacognitive bias when predicting the reminder bias) (β=–0.04, SE = 0.04, t=–0.94, p=0.35).
source: Finally, we preregistered to run the same analysis for the AD factor without hypothesising about any specific direction for any potential effects. However, we did not find evidence for a moderation effect (an interaction between AD scores and metacognitive bias when predicting the reminder bias), β=–0.04, SE = 0.04, t=–0.94, p=0.35, controlling for age, gender, and educational attainment (see Appendix 1—table 12).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support.

claim: There was no support for the Metacognitive Control Mechanism (as would be reflected in a disrupted link between confidence and offloading).
source: In summary, whilst we found no support for the Metacognitive Control Mechanism (as would be reflected in a disrupted link between confidence and offloading), we did find support for both the Metacognitive Monitoring Mechanism (reduced pro-reminder bias as a downstream consequence of overconfidence) and the Direct Mechanism (independent contribution of CIT on offloading).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of findings.

claim: There was support for the Metacognitive Monitoring Mechanism (reduced pro-reminder bias as a downstream consequence of overconfidence).
source: In summary, whilst we found no support for the Metacognitive Control Mechanism (as would be reflected in a disrupted link between confidence and offloading), we did find support for both the Metacognitive Monitoring Mechanism (reduced pro-reminder bias as a downstream consequence of overconfidence) and the Direct Mechanism (independent contribution of CIT on offloading).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of findings.

claim: There was support for the Direct Mechanism (independent contribution of CIT on offloading).
source: In summary, whilst we found no support for the Metacognitive Control Mechanism (as would be reflected in a disrupted link between confidence and offloading), we did find support for both the Metacognitive Monitoring Mechanism (reduced pro-reminder bias as a downstream consequence of overconfidence) and the Direct Mechanism (independent contribution of CIT on offloading).

source: Contrary to our hypotheses, however, we found that compulsivity was linked reduced offloading, and that this effect was only in part explained by overconfidence.

claim: Perfectionism may explain why some compulsive individuals avoid using reminders altogether due to rigid, perfectionistic beliefs about needing to remember everything without relying on external aids.
source: One possible interpretation is perfectionism: Some compulsive individuals may avoid using reminders altogether due to rigid, perfectionistic beliefs about needing to remember everything without relying on external aids, and using reminders could trigger their anxiety or feed into their obsessions about being forgetful or unreliable.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible interpretation of the findings.

claim: Perfectionism serves as a transdiagnostic maintaining and risk factor for various mental health conditions, including compulsive disorders like eating disorders and OCD.
source: This interpretation aligns with findings, suggesting that perfectionism serves as a transdiagnostic maintaining and risk factor for various mental health conditions, including compulsive disorders like eating disorders and OCD (Egan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Kirk et al., 2021 found no effect of anxiety on offloading.
source: This aligns with a recent study by Kirk et al., 2021, which also found no effect of anxiety on offloading.

claim: Kirk et al., 2021 found no relative underconfidence among anxious participants.
source: However, their study, which used the 'trait' component of the STAI to measure anxiety (Spielberger et al., 1983), found no relative underconfidence among anxious participants either.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The transdiagnostic approach likely revealed the confidence effect by separating the counteracting influences of AD and CIT factors.
source: Our transdiagnostic approach likely revealed this confidence effect by separating the counteracting influences of AD and CIT factors.

claim: Mohr et al., 2024 observed that while high-AD participants were underconfident in a perceptual task, this underconfidence did not lead to increased information-seeking behaviour.
source: Our findings align with those reported in a recent study by Mohr et al., 2024. The authors observed that while high-AD participants were underconfident in a perceptual task, this underconfidence did not lead to increased information-seeking behaviour.

claim: The study did not find the impaired confidence-action link reported for transdiagnostic compulsivity and OCD patients in prior work.
source: Contrary to Seow and Gillan, 2020, and Vaghi et al., 2017, our study did not find the impaired confidence-action link (Metacognitive Control Mechanism) reported for transdiagnostic compulsivity and OCD patients.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by the non-significant interaction effect in the results.

claim: The lack of finding an impaired confidence-action link may be because of differences between tasks – prior work used a reinforcement learning task with a clear learning element from trial to trial.
source: This may be because of differences between tasks – prior work used a reinforcement learning task with a clear learning element from trial to trial.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible explanation for the discrepancy with prior findings.

claim: It is possible the study was underpowered to detect the confidence-action link, as the sample size was designed to detect overconfidence in compulsivity, not the more nuanced confidence-action link.
source: Alternatively, it is possible our study was underpowered, as our sample size was designed to detect overconfidence in compulsivity, not the more nuanced but still psychometrically robust confidence-action link (Loosen et al., 2022), which would have required a far larger sample size.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible explanation for the null finding.

source: Recent studies also failed to find decreased action-confidence coupling with relatively small groups of OCD patients and controls (Hoven et al., 2023b; Marzuki et al., 2022).

Based on this, we excluded 40 participants.

claim: The study split the accuracy data to avoid circularity, including only the even trials to calculate the ACCFI for the OIP, whereas only the odd trials were included to calculate the ACCFI for the metacognitive bias.
source: Crucially, our study relies on the key assumption that the metacognitive bias can predict the reminder bias, but ACCFI contributes to both biases. To avoid circularity, we therefore split the accuracy data to avoid potentially inflating the correlation. More specifically, we included only the even trials to calculate the ACCFI for the OIP, whereas we included only the odd trials to calculate the ACCFI for the metacognitive bias.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
